menachot-7a-7-11.note: Avimi, Rav Hisda's teacher, had forgotten tractate Menahot, so he went to his own student Rav Hisda to relearn it, thinking that making the effort to travel would help him remember. On his way back, Rav Nahman met him and asked how a priest removes a handful from a meal offering; Avimi pointed to a vessel on the ground. Asked whether one may use a vessel resting on the ground, Avimi said a priest would first lift it, and he answered the same about placing the offering in a vessel. When Rav Nahman objected that this needs three priests, Avimi replied: let it need thirteen, like the daily offering.
menachot-7a-7-11.why: Rabbi Zeira has said the question whether a vessel resting on the ground can be used for a meal offering arose when Avimi studied at Rav Hisda's; the Gemara first asks how a teacher came to study with his student, then gives the exchange.

people.name: Avimi
people.about: Rav Hisda's teacher, who forgot a tractate and relearned it from his student.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Avimi's student, who says Avimi once gave him many blows of mockery over a ruling.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who meets Avimi and questions him about meal offerings.

terms.meaning: A Temple offering of flour, often with oil and frankincense; a handful is burned on the altar and the rest eaten by priests.
The rite in which a priest scoops a handful of the meal offering to burn on the altar.
Here, placing the offering in a sacred Temple vessel, which makes it holy for the service.
The lamb offered every morning and afternoon in the Temple, whose service involved thirteen priests.

menachot-15a-15-15.note: A man sowed seeds in someone else's vineyard while the grapes on the vines were just budding. The case came before the Sages, who ruled the seeds forbidden, because of the ban on growing mixed crops in a vineyard, but left the vines permitted.
menachot-15a-15-15.why: Rav has ruled that a thanks offering's loaves can be disqualified though the offering is not; the Gemara asks why an argument from lighter to weightier does not spare the loaves, since this ruling seems to reject such an argument, then rejects the comparison.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the mixed produce becomes forbidden for any use.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.

menachot-15b-5-5.note: A man sowed seeds in his friend's vineyard while the grapes on the vines were just budding. The case came before the Sages, who ruled the seeds forbidden, because of the ban on growing mixed crops in a vineyard, but left the vines permitted.
menachot-15b-5-5.why: In a second version of Rabbi Elazar's question, about the Shavuot lambs and loaves, Rav rules the loaves can be disqualified though the lambs are not; the Gemara challenges this with the vineyard ruling, which seems to reject such an argument, then answers it.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the mixed produce becomes forbidden for any use.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.

menachot-18a-3-6.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells how he went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and found Yosef the Babylonian there, who loved every ruling he heard. Yosef asked whether an offering slaughtered with the intent to leave some of its blood until the next day is fit; Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua said it was fit, and Yosef asked again that evening, the next morning, at noon and in the afternoon, until Rabbi Elazar added that Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit, and Yosef's face lit up. Yosef explained that Rabbi Yehuda had taught him it was unfit, and none of Rabbi Yehuda's other disciples had heard it; now his lost teaching was restored. Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua wept, praised scholars who love Torah, and said that Rabbi Yehuda learned this through his father from Rabbi Eliezer.
menachot-18a-3-6.why: The Gemara has said that in Rabbi Yehuda's view everyone agrees intent to leave the blood until the next day disqualifies an offering; it cites this account to challenge that, then works out what Rabbi Yehuda actually taught Yosef.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who tells the story of his visit to Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
people.about: The teacher Yosef questions again and again; he weeps at Yosef's love of Torah.

people.name: Yosef the Babylonian
people.about: A student who had learned a ruling from Rabbi Yehuda that no one else seemed to know.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Yosef's earlier teacher; son of Rabbi Elai, who was a student of Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who held the offering unfit, the source of Rabbi Yehuda's teaching.

terms.meaning: Of a sacrifice: valid, properly offered and acceptable.
What the priest has in mind while slaughtering; a wrong plan, such as delaying the blood rites past their time, can disqualify an offering.
Here, a teaching as passed down from a particular Sage.

menachot-29a-18-18.note: Agra, the father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, found that in his phylacteries the leg of the letter heh in the word "the nation" had been cut off by a small hole in the parchment. He went to his son-in-law Rabbi Abba to ask whether they were still usable. Rabbi Abba told him that if the part of the leg still attached to the top of the letter was as long as a small letter, they were fit; if not, they were unfit.
menachot-29a-18-18.why: The Gemara has just reported a ruling in Rav Yehuda's name that a heh whose leg is perforated is fit only if a small letter's length remains; this case shows the ruling applied in practice.

people.name: Agra
people.about: Rabbi Abba's father-in-law, whose phylacteries had a damaged letter

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Agra's son-in-law, whom Agra asked for a ruling

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding handwritten Torah passages, worn on the arm and head during prayer; every letter in them must be written properly.
A letter of the Hebrew alphabet whose left leg stands slightly apart from its roof.

menachot-29b-2-4.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that when Moses went up on High he found God tying little crowns onto the letters of the Torah. God explained that a man named Akiva ben Yosef would one day derive heaps of laws from every stroke of them. Moses asked to see him, sat at the back of Rabbi Akiva's study hall, understood nothing and lost heart, until a student asked Rabbi Akiva for his source and he answered that it was a law given to Moses at Sinai, which put Moses at ease. Moses asked why God would give the Torah through him and not this man, and then asked to see Akiva's reward; he saw Akiva's flesh being weighed in a butcher shop. To each protest God said: Be silent; this is what arose in My thought.
menachot-29b-2-4.why: The Gemara has been discussing how exactly the letters of phylacteries and mezuzot must be formed; this story about the crowns on the letters leads into Rava's list of which letters need crowns and how scribes shaped them.

people.name: Moses
people.about: Goes up on High to receive the Torah and questions God

people.name: Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who is tying crowns on the letters and answers Moses

people.name: Akiva ben Yosef
people.about: Rabbi Akiva, the future Sage who will derive many laws from the crowns; Moses sees him teach and then sees his death

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name the story is told

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the story in Rav's name

terms.meaning: Small decorative strokes that scribes add to the tops of certain letters in a Torah scroll.

terms.term: a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai
terms.meaning: A law with no written source in the Torah, held to have been given orally to Moses at Mount Sinai.
Jewish laws; the plural of halakha.

menachot-31a-3-3.note: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri tells that some of his untithed produce once got mixed into a larger amount of produce that had already been tithed. He went to ask Rabbi Tarfon what to do. Rabbi Tarfon told him to go buy produce in the market, which may or may not have been tithed, and to separate the tithes from that produce on behalf of the mixture.
menachot-31a-3-3.why: The Gemara has been listing rulings of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri; after this one it explains Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning, which turns on whether by Torah law the small amount of untithed produce is cancelled out in the larger mixture.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
people.about: Tells this story about his own produce

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage whom Rabbi Shimon Shezuri asked for a ruling

terms.meaning: Crops from which the required portions for priests, Levites and the poor have not yet been set aside, and so may not be eaten.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

menachot-31b-8-9.note: Rabbi Helbo reports that he saw Rav Huna roll up a mezuza from its last word back toward its first, and write its two passages in the "closed" style, with the second passage starting on the same line where the first ended. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who reports that Rabbi Meir wrote a mezuza on the inner layer of hide, shaped like a narrow column, with space above and below, and in the "open" style, starting the second passage on a new line. When he asked his teacher why, Rabbi Meir said it was because the two passages are not next to each other in the Torah.
menachot-31b-8-9.why: The Gemara is working through how a mezuza must be laid out; Rav Huna's practice is challenged by Rabbi Meir's, and the Gemara goes on to ask which one Rav's ruling follows, settling that custom now favors the closed style.

people.name: Rabbi Helbo
people.about: Reports what he saw Rav Huna do

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Wrote and rolled a mezuza in the way Rabbi Helbo describes

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Student of Rabbi Meir who reports his teacher's practice and asked him the reason

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Wrote mezuzot in the open style and explained why

terms.meaning: A small parchment with two Torah passages, rolled up and fixed to a doorpost.
Two ways of separating sections of text: closed means the next section begins on the same line after a gap; open means it begins on a new line.
The inner layer of an animal hide, used as a writing surface.

menachot-32b-5-5.note: Rav Helbo reports that he saw Rav Huna about to sit on his bed while a Torah scroll lay on it. Rav Huna first turned a jug upside down on the ground, set the Torah scroll on it, and only then sat on the bed.
menachot-32b-5-5.why: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna held it forbidden to sit on a bed with a Torah scroll on it, and then notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Yohanan, who permits it.

people.name: Rav Helbo
people.about: Reports what he saw Rav Huna do

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Moved a Torah scroll off his bed before sitting on it

terms.meaning: The handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, treated with great reverence.

menachot-35a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that a student of Rabbi Akiva used to tie his phylacteries with strips of sky-blue wool instead of leather, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing to him. Someone asked whether that righteous man could really have seen his student do this and not object. Another Sage answered: yes, it could be that the student was wrong, because Rabbi Akiva never saw him; had he seen it, he would not have allowed it.
menachot-35a-6-6.why: The Gemara quotes this from a baraita that requires phylacteries to be tied only with straps of hide; it is raised as an objection to Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling that the straps must be black.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Tells the incident

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The teacher who did not object, because, the answer goes, he never saw it

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding Torah passages, tied to the arm and head with straps during prayer.
Wool dyed with a costly blue dye, used for one of the strings of ritual fringes.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

menachot-35a-7-7.note: Hyrcanus, the son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, used to tie his phylacteries with strips of purple wool, and his father said nothing to him. Someone asked whether that righteous man could have seen his son do this and not object. The Sages answered: yes, it could be that the son was wrong, because Rabbi Eliezer never saw him; had he seen it, he would not have allowed it.
menachot-35a-7-7.why: This is the second incident in a baraita teaching that phylacteries must be tied with straps of hide; the Gemara raises the baraita against Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling that straps must be black, and answers that the black is required on the outside.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: Son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who tied his phylacteries with purple wool

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus
people.about: His father, who said nothing, because, the Sages answer, he never saw it

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding Torah passages, tied to the arm and head with straps during prayer.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

menachot-37a-6-6.note: The Sage Peleimu asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on which head a man with two heads should put his phylacteries. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him either to go into exile or accept excommunication for such a question. Just then a man arrived saying a firstborn son with two heads had been born to him, and asked how much he must give the priest to redeem him. An elder came and told him he had to give ten sela, five for each head.
menachot-37a-6-6.why: The Gemara has been asking where on the head phylacteries go; afterwards it questions the elder's ruling, since a child unlikely to live is normally not redeemed, and answers that the verse ties the redemption to each skull.

people.name: Peleimu
people.about: A Sage who asked the two-headed question

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who rebuked Peleimu for the question

people.name: a certain elder
people.about: Ruled that the father of the two-headed firstborn must pay ten sela

terms.meaning: A formal ban by which a person is shunned by the community.
A father's duty to pay a priest five silver coins for his firstborn son.
A silver coin; five were paid to redeem a firstborn.

menachot-37b-14-14.note: Ravina was walking behind Mar bar Rav Ashi on the Shabbat of a Festival when the corner of Mar bar Rav Ashi's garment, where one of his ritual fringes hung, tore off. Ravina said nothing until they reached Mar bar Rav Ashi's house, and then told him it had torn back on the road. Mar bar Rav Ashi said that if Ravina had told him there, he would have thrown the garment off right there.
menachot-37b-14-14.why: The Gemara has just said the law does not follow Rabbi Yishmael, who held each fringe stands alone; this incident shows a garment missing one fringe treated as unfit to wear outdoors on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks why human dignity did not permit it.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Walked behind Mar bar Rav Ashi and waited to tell him about the tear

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Whose garment tore; said he would have thrown it off

terms.meaning: Strings tied to each of the four corners of a garment, as the Torah commands; if one corner lacks them, the garment does not fulfill the commandment.
A Sabbath during a festival, when carrying in a public place is forbidden.

menachot-38a-0-1.note: In another version of the incident, Ravina told Mar bar Rav Ashi, at the very place where it happened, that the corner of his garment had torn. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered: do you think I should throw it off? Doesn't the Master say that human dignity is so great that it overrides a prohibition of the Torah?
menachot-38a-0-1.why: The Gemara is asking how a Sage could keep wearing a garment he was not allowed to carry. In this version he knew and relied on human dignity, and the Gemara explains that this works because the place was a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who tells Mar bar Rav Ashi that his garment has torn.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose garment tore while he was walking.

people.name: Rav bar Shabba
people.about: A Sage who explained before Rav Kahana that human dignity overrides only rabbinic prohibitions.

terms.meaning: The principle that a person need not shame himself in public; the Gemara says it overrides rules made by the Sages, not those written in the Torah.
An area that is neither fully public nor private, where carrying on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

menachot-39a-11-11.note: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana were sitting together when a man passed by wearing a cloak made entirely of sky-blue wool, with white and sky-blue ritual fringes that were wound all the way down, with no loose strands hanging. Rav said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not. Rabba bar bar Hana said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.
menachot-39a-11-11.why: The Gemara has just set rules for how the fringe strings are wound; their two remarks become a disagreement over whether fringes must also have loose strings hanging below the windings, which the Gemara then traces to two verses.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who said the cloak was beautiful but the fringes were not.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav who said both the cloak and the fringes were beautiful.

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment (tzitzit), including a sky-blue thread.
A blue dye (tekhelet) the Torah requires for one thread of the fringes.
Sets of coils wrapped around the fringe strings near the garment.

menachot-41a-7-9.note: Rabba bar Huna visited Rava bar Rav Nahman and saw him wearing a cloak folded in half, with fringes tied at the corners of the fold. The cloak unfolded and the fringe ended up near his head, in the middle of the cloak. Rabba bar Huna told him this was not the corner the Torah speaks of. Rava bar Rav Nahman threw the cloak off and put on a different one. Rabba bar Huna then told him that fringes are not a duty on the man but on every cloak he owns, so he should go and put fringes on it properly.
menachot-41a-7-9.why: The Gemara has just discussed whether a folded cloak needs fringes at its fold; this case raises the wider question of whether fringes are a duty of the person or of the garment, which the Gemara goes on to test.

people.name: Rabba bar Huna
people.about: Visitor who pointed out the misplaced fringe

people.name: Rava bar Rav Nahman
people.about: His host, who wore the folded cloak

terms.meaning: Strings the Torah commands to be tied to each of the four corners of a garment.

menachot-41a-11-12.note: An angel found Rav Ketina wearing a linen cloak and said to him: Ketina, Ketina! A linen cloak in summer and a two-cornered coat in winter, garments that both need no fringes. What will become of the sky-blue fringes? Rav Ketina asked whether they punish even for failing to do a positive commandment. The angel answered that at a time of divine anger, they do punish.
menachot-41a-11-12.why: The Gemara says the angel's words disagree with Rabba bar Huna, who held that fringes are a duty on every garment owned; it then argues over what the angel's rebuke shows, concluding he was charging Rav Ketina with looking for ways to avoid the commandment.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who wore garments exempt from fringes

people.name: an angel
people.about: Rebuked Rav Ketina for avoiding the commandment of fringes

terms.meaning: A commandment to do something, as opposed to one forbidding an act.
Ritual fringes with one string dyed a costly blue.

menachot-42a-8-9.note: Ravina and Rav Samma were sitting before Rav Ashi. Rav Samma saw that the corner of Ravina's cloak had torn, leaving the hole for the fringes closer to the edge than a thumb joint, and asked whether Ravina did not follow Rabbi Ya'akov's ruling. Ravina answered that the distance is required only when the fringes are made. Rav Samma was embarrassed, and Rav Ashi told him not to be upset: one of them is like two of us.
menachot-42a-8-9.why: The Gemara has just explained why both Rav Pappa's and Rabbi Ya'akov's rulings on where to put the fringe hole are needed; this exchange clarifies that Rabbi Ya'akov's minimum distance applies when the fringes are attached, not after a later tear.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Whose cloak corner had torn; explained when the rule applies

people.name: Rav Samma
people.about: Questioned Ravina and was embarrassed by the answer

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The teacher they sat before, who consoled Rav Samma

terms.meaning: A measure of length, the width of the top joint of the thumb.

menachot-43a-3-4.note: In the time of Rav Ahai, Mar from Mashkhei brought some sky-blue wool. It was tested by Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda's method and its color faded, then by Rav Adda's method and its color improved. The Sages thought to declare it unfit. Rav Ahai told them it cannot be neither true blue dye nor indigo; so the two tests must have been stated together, as one procedure.
menachot-43a-3-4.why: The Gemara has just quoted two separate tests for real sky-blue dye; this case shows they can disagree, and Rav Ahai's conclusion turns them into two steps of one test, which word from the Land of Israel later confirms.

people.name: Mar from Mashkhei
people.about: A Sage who brought the sky-blue wool

people.name: Rav Ahai
people.about: The leading Sage of the time, who resolved the conflict between the tests

terms.meaning: The true sky-blue dye required for ritual fringes, taken from a sea creature; cheaper indigo looks the same.
A plant dye that looks like the true sky-blue but is not valid for fringes.

menachot-44a-3-10.note: A man careful about ritual fringes paid a prostitute overseas four hundred gold coins. She laid out seven beds, and sat naked on the top one. As he climbed up to join her, his four fringes struck him on the face, and he dropped to the ground; so did she, and she swore not to let him go until he told her what defect he saw in her. He swore she was the most beautiful woman he had seen, but the fringes appeared to him like four witnesses against him. She had him write down his name, city, teacher and study hall, divided up her property, and came to Rabbi Hiyya asking to convert. When he asked if she had her eye on a student, she showed him the note, and he told her to go take her purchase. The beds she had spread for him forbiddenly she now spread for him permitted.
menachot-44a-3-10.why: Rabbi Natan has just taught that every commandment in the Torah carries a reward in this world, with the reward in the World-to-Come unknown; this story is his proof, and it closes by repeating that point.

people.name: a certain man
people.about: Careful about ritual fringes; his fringes stopped him from sinning

people.name: the prostitute
people.about: The woman overseas who later came to Rabbi Hiyya to convert

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Head of the study hall where she asked to convert

terms.meaning: Strings tied to the four corners of a garment, which the Torah says are to remind the wearer of the commandments.
An oath by something Roman; the text does not explain what the gappa is.
A non-Jew who formally joins the Jewish people.

menachot-45a-18-18.note: Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that a man named Hanina ben Hizkiyya should be remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been withdrawn, since parts of it seemed to contradict the Torah. He carried three hundred jugs of oil up to his upper room, sat there, and interpreted the book until the contradictions were resolved.
menachot-45a-18-18.why: The Gemara has been working through verses in Ezekiel that seem to clash with Torah law about offerings; this statement closes that discussion.

people.name: Hanina ben Hizkiyya
people.about: Interpreted the book of Ezekiel so that it was not withdrawn

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name the praise is said

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports it in Rav's name

terms.meaning: Hidden away and kept out of use, here meaning left out of the Bible.

menachot-51b-19-20.note: When a High Priest died and no successor had yet been appointed, his daily meal offering still had to be brought. At first it was paid for from public Temple funds, as the Torah requires. When the Sages saw the Temple treasury running low, they made the dead priest's heirs pay instead. When they saw the heirs neglecting it, they went back to paying from public funds.
menachot-51b-19-20.why: A mishna lists public payment for this offering as one of seven rabbinic enactments, which seems to make it rabbinic rather than Torah law. Rabbi Abbahu answers that it is Torah law; the Sages changed it and then restored it, which is why it is listed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel around 300 CE, based in Caesarea.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple in Jerusalem, who brought a special offering of flat cakes of flour and oil every day.
The Temple treasury room, holding funds collected from the whole people to pay for public offerings.
A rule enacted by the Sages, as distinct from one written in the Torah itself.

menachot-53a-12-18.note: The Sages told Rabbi Perida that Rabbi Ezra, a descendant of Ezra the Scribe through a long line of famous Sages, was waiting at his gate. Rabbi Perida asked why they were listing his ancestors: a man of Torah is worthy on his own, but a man of lineage without Torah, "better for fire to devour him" than enter. Told that Ezra was a man of Torah, he let him in. Seeing Ezra was troubled, Rabbi Perida taught a homily praising the Patriarchs as those whom God credits. Hearing the word "excellent" (addir), Rabbi Ezra replied with a series of wordplay homilies on addir, yadid (beloved), "good" and "this," each tying Moses, Solomon, Abraham, the Torah, the Temple, God and Israel together.
menachot-53a-12-18.why: Rabbi Perida has just appeared in the discussion asking where meal offerings get their rule against leavening, so the Gemara attaches this incident about him.

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: A Sage at whose house Rabbi Ezra waited; he insisted that Torah learning, not lineage, makes a man worthy.

people.name: Rabbi Ezra
people.about: A Sage descended from Ezra the Scribe, who answered Rabbi Perida with homilies of his own.

people.name: Ezra
people.about: Ezra the Scribe, Rabbi Ezra's ancestor.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A Sage in Rabbi Ezra's family line, descended from Ezra the Scribe.

people.name: Rabbi Avtolus
people.about: Rabbi Ezra's grandfather, a descendant of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

terms.meaning: A sermon-like reading of Bible verses that draws a lesson from wording, often through wordplay.
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the founding fathers of the Jewish people.

menachot-64b-4-6.note: During a civil war between Hasmonean kings, Hyrcanus besieged Jerusalem from outside and Aristoblus held it from inside. Each day those inside let down coins in a box and those outside sent up animals for the daily offerings. An old man who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers in coded language that as long as the Temple service went on, the city would not fall to them. The next day they sent up a pig. When it reached halfway up the wall it dug its hooves in, and the Land of Israel shook for four hundred parasangs in each direction. Then the Sages said: Cursed is he who raises pigs, and cursed is he who teaches his son Greek wisdom.
menachot-64b-4-6.why: The mishna mentions that once the omer barley came from Gaggot Tzerifin, far from Jerusalem; this baraita explains that it happened in this war, when the fields near the city were ruined.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: Hasmonean king who besieged Jerusalem from outside

people.name: Aristoblus
people.about: Hasmonean king who held Jerusalem from inside

people.name: a certain elderly man
people.about: Knew Greek wisdom and gave the besiegers the idea that stopped the offerings

terms.meaning: The Jewish royal dynasty whose kings here fought each other.
The two lambs offered in the Temple every day, morning and afternoon.
A measure of new barley brought to the Temple as an offering in spring.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles.

menachot-64b-7-7.note: When it was time to bring the omer, no one knew where to find barley for it, so it was announced publicly. A deaf-mute came and put one hand on a roof and the other on a hut. Mordekhai asked whether there was a place called Gaggot Tzerifin, which means "roofs of huts". They checked and found it.
menachot-64b-7-7.why: The mishna records that the omer once came from Gaggot Tzerifin; the Gemara has told how war ruined the fields near Jerusalem, and this tradition tells how the distant place was found.

people.name: a certain deaf-mute
people.about: Pointed to a roof and a hut, hinting at the place name

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: Read the deaf-mute's gestures as the name of a place

terms.meaning: A measure of new barley reaped and brought to the Temple as an offering in spring.
A person who can neither hear nor speak, who here communicates by gestures.

menachot-64b-8-8.note: In a time when the fields around Jerusalem had been ruined, the court did not know where to find wheat for the two loaves offered on Shavuot, and made a public proclamation. A deaf-mute man came forward and put one hand on his eye and the other on a door latch. Mordekhai asked the Sages whether there was a place called Ein Sokher ('eye' and 'latch') or Sokher Ayin. They checked, found such a place, and brought the wheat from its fields.
menachot-64b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that during the civil war that ruined the land, the omer barley came from Gaggot Tzerifin and the two loaves from Ein Sokher. This story, paired with the one about the omer before it, tells how the second place was found.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who works out the meaning of the deaf-mute's gestures.

terms.meaning: A Temple offering of two loaves of bread made from the new wheat crop, brought on the festival of Shavuot.
A person who can neither hear nor speak; here he communicates only by pointing.

menachot-64b-9-11.note: Three women brought three pairs of birds as offerings. One said hers was "for my ziva," one "for my yamma," and one "for my ona." The Sages took all three to mean bleeding and purification, so each would bring a sin offering and a burnt offering. Mordekhai suggested instead that one had been in danger from a flow, one at sea (yam), and one through her eye (ayin), so all three were thanksgiving burnt offerings. It was checked, and Mordekhai was found to be right.
menachot-64b-9-11.why: The Gemara has just told how Mordekhai decoded a deaf-mute's gestures to find grain for the Temple; this is a further example of his skill with words, and leads to identifying him with Petahya, who was in charge of bird offerings.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who read the women's words differently from the other Sages and was found to be right.

terms.meaning: Pairs of pigeons or doves brought as offerings, for example by a woman after certain kinds of bleeding.
A woman with a discharge of blood outside her normal period, who must bring an offering when she is purified.
A sin offering atones for a specific state or wrong; a burnt offering is burned whole on the altar and can also be a voluntary gift.

menachot-65a-11-11.note: When the Boethusians claimed that Shavuot must always fall on a Sunday, Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai joined the debate: 'Fools! From where do you get this?' No one answered except one old man, who prattled that Moses loved Israel and, knowing Shavuot is only one day, set it after Shabbat so the people could enjoy two days in a row. Rabban Yoḥanan quoted the verse that the journey from Horeb takes eleven days, and asked why, if Moses loved Israel, he kept them in the wilderness forty years. The old man protested, 'My teacher, you dismiss me with this?' Rabban Yoḥanan replied: 'Fool! Will our perfect Torah not be as worthy as your idle talk?'
menachot-65a-11-11.why: The Gemara is explaining a list of dates on which eulogies were forbidden; the days from the eighth of Nisan to the end of Passover mark when the correct date of Shavuot was restored against the Boethusians. After this exchange Rabban Yoḥanan gives a real proof from the verses.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who challenges the Boethusians.

people.name: the elderly man
people.about: The only one of the Boethusians who answers him.

people.name: Moses
people.about: The old man claims Moses set Shavuot after Shabbat out of love for the people.

terms.meaning: A group that rejected the Sages' tradition and read 'the morrow after the day of rest' literally as Sunday, so that Shavuot would always fall on a Sunday.
The festival held seven weeks (fifty days) after the start of the omer count at Passover.

menachot-68b-13-13.note: Rabbi Tarfon sat puzzling over why meal offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit, while those brought before the two loaves are fit. Yehuda ben Nehemya answered him with a distinction, Rabbi Tarfon fell silent, and the young man's face lit up. Rabbi Akiva said to him: "Yehuda, has your face brightened because you answered the elder? I will be astonished if your life is long." Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai reported that this happened two weeks before Passover; when he came back for Shavuot and asked about Yehuda ben Nehemya, he was told he had died.
menachot-68b-13-13.why: The mishna rules that offerings from new grain brought before the omer are unfit but those brought between the omer and the two loaves are fit; the incident gives the reasoning for that difference, which Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak then extends to fruit.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: An elder Sage who raised the question and fell silent at the answer.

people.name: Yehuda ben Nehemya
people.about: A Sage who answered Rabbi Tarfon and looked pleased; he died soon afterward.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who rebuked Yehuda ben Nehemya for gloating over answering the elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ilai
people.about: A Sage who tells when the incident happened and that Yehuda ben Nehemya died.

terms.meaning: A measure of new barley offered in the Temple on the second day of Passover; only after it may the new crop be eaten.
Two wheat loaves offered on Shavuot, after which the new crop may be used for Temple offerings.
An offering of flour, usually mixed with oil, brought in the Temple.

menachot-69b-1-1.note: Ulla reported, in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yehotzadak, an incident on the east bank of the Jordan in which wolves swallowed two children and excreted them. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the flesh was ritually pure.
menachot-69b-1-1.why: The Gemara is asking whether palm leaves swallowed whole by an elephant count as digested, so that a basket woven from them is like a dung vessel that cannot become impure. This incident is offered as an answer, but the Gemara rejects it because flesh is soft and leaves are hard.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Yehotzadak
people.about: The Sage in whose name Ulla reports it.

terms.meaning: Not carrying ritual impurity. Human remains normally impart impurity; the Sages ruled that flesh which had passed through the wolves no longer did.

menachot-85b-13-17.note: The people of Laodicea needed oil and sent a messenger to buy a million maneh worth. Jerusalem sent him to Tyre, Tyre to Gush Ḥalav, and there he was sent to a man hoeing under his olive trees, who told him to wait until he finished. Seeing the man carry his tools and clear stones as he walked, the messenger thought the Jews were mocking him. But at home a maidservant brought hot water and a golden basin of oil, and the man dipped his hands and feet in it. After they ate, he measured out the oil, then another 180,000 maneh worth on credit, and came along to collect. The messenger hired every horse, mule, camel and donkey in the land; when his city came out to praise him, he told them to praise the man who came with him.
menachot-85b-13-17.why: The Gemara has been discussing Tekoa, the main source of oil for meal offerings. It turns to a teaching that Moses' blessing of Asher, 'and dip his foot in oil', describes oil flowing like a spring in Asher's land, and this story shows it.

people.name: the messenger
people.about: Sent by the people of Laodicea to buy oil.

people.name: the olive grower
people.about: A man of Gush Ḥalav who looks like a poor laborer but supplies all the oil.

people.name: his maidservant
people.about: Brings him hot water and a golden basin of oil.

terms.meaning: A unit of money; the amounts in the story are given in maneh worth of oil.
A town the text places in the tribal portion of Asher.

menachot-93b-14-16.note: Rabbi Elazar repeated Reish Lakish's teaching, that where the Torah says 'his hand' it means two hands, in the study hall without saying it in Reish Lakish's name. Reish Lakish heard and became angry. He challenged him: if 'his hand' means two, why does the Torah ever write 'his hands'? He raised twenty-four such verses against him, and Rabbi Elazar was silent. After Reish Lakish calmed down, he asked him why he had not answered that the rule was only about 'his hands' in the rite of placing hands.
menachot-93b-14-16.why: The mishna requires placing both hands on an offering. Reish Lakish derived this from the Yom Kippur verse and made it a general rule; this episode tests that rule and narrows it to the rite of placing hands.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Taught Reish Lakish's rule without naming its source.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The author of the rule, angry at not being credited.

terms.meaning: A rite in which the person bringing an animal offering presses his hands on its head before it is slaughtered.
The house of study where the Sages taught and debated.

menachot-100a-8-8.note: Once the light of the moon rose, and the priests imagined that the eastern sky was lit by the sunrise. They slaughtered the daily offering, and then had to take it out to the place of burning.
menachot-100a-8-8.why: The Gemara quotes a mishna about Yom Kippur in which a lookout had to confirm that the whole eastern sky was lit, as far as Hebron, before the daily offering was slaughtered. This incident is the reason given for that practice.

terms.meaning: A lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon. It may not be slaughtered at night.
The place where offerings that had become unfit were taken to be burned.

menachot-103b-18-20.note: Rabbi Beivai reported, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that a mule belonging to the household of Rabbi died and the Sages estimated its blood at a quarter-log. Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna objected with a testimony that a carcass's blood is pure, and with an incident told by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira: wild donkeys were killed to feed the lions in the king's stadium, pilgrims waded in their blood up to the knees, and the Sages said nothing to them. Rabbi Beivai fell silent. When Rabbi Zerika asked why, he said his life was like the verse 'you shall have no assurance of your life', which Rabbi Hanin read as one who relies on a baker for bread; he relied on a baker. Rav Yosef later explained that Rabbi Yehuda, decisor for the Nasi's house, ruled by his own tradition.
menachot-103b-18-20.why: The Gemara has been showing that the Sages' measures are exact, down to a hair; the mule's blood adds the quarter-log measure, and the objection asks whether a carcass's blood makes anyone impure at all.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident of the mule and cannot answer the objection to it.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: The Sage who objects that a carcass's blood is pure.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: The Sage who asks Rabbi Beivai why he does not answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira
people.about: An early Sage who told of pilgrims wading in donkeys' blood without the Sages objecting.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who explains that Rabbi Yehuda ruled for the Nasi's house by his own tradition that such blood is impure.

terms.meaning: A small liquid measure, the minimum amount of blood that can make a person or thing ritually impure.
An animal that died without proper ritual slaughter; its flesh makes people ritually impure.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held this office.

menachot-109b-9-15.note: Shimon HaTzaddik, the High Priest, foresaw his death: each Yom Kippur an old man in white had entered the Holy of Holies with him and left with him, but this year he was in black and did not leave. He died after Sukkot, naming his son Onias as successor. In Rabbi Meir's telling, Onias's older brother Shimi, jealous, tricked Onias into a tunic and ribbon and told the priests it was a vow to his lover; the priests wanted to kill Onias, who fled to Alexandria and built an altar for idol worship. Rabbi Yehuda says it was the reverse: Onias declined the post, then grew jealous and played the trick on Shimi; when exposed he fled to Alexandria and built an altar to God. The Sages drew a lesson about jealousy over high office.
menachot-109b-9-15.why: The mishna implies the temple of Onias in Egypt was not for idol worship; this baraita is cited because Rabbi Yehuda's version supports that view, while Rabbi Meir's says it was.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest who foresaw his own death and named his son Onias to succeed him.

people.name: Onias
people.about: Son of Shimon HaTzaddik, who built an altar in Alexandria in Egypt.

people.name: Shimi
people.about: Onias's brother, two and a half years older than him.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose version says Onias's altar was for idol worship.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says the incident went otherwise and Onias's altar was for God.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, on Yom Kippur.
The blessing the priests recite over the people; in the Temple it was said with God's own name.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

menachot-104a-0-1.note: Rabbi Beivai, explaining why he could not answer an objection, ends by saying that he is a man who relies on the baker for his bread, the most anxious of the three kinds of people in Rabbi Ḥanin's reading of the curse, and so in no state to answer. The Gemara asks what was concluded, and Rav Yosef says that Rabbi Yehuda was the halakhic decisor of the house of the Nasi and instructed them according to his own tradition, that the blood of a carcass is impure.
menachot-104a-0-1.why: The question was why the Sages measured the blood of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's dead mule when a carcass's blood had been testified to be pure. Rav Yosef's answer resolves it, and the Gemara backs it with Rabbi Yehuda's report that Beit Hillel deem such blood impure from a quarter-log.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: The Sage who could not answer the objection.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Gives the Gemara's resolution.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The halakhic decisor of the house of the Nasi, who ruled by his own tradition.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' is his household.
The authority who gives rulings on Jewish law.
